Oppelt et al. [@oppelt2018model] measured the response to TNFα not only in untreated cells but
also with drugs known to cause liver injury: diclofenac (DCF) with the imaging and blots of the
first chapters, and amiodarone (AMD), paracetamol (APAP), fialuridine (FIAU) and ximelagatran
(XIM) with four blots. The question is which processes of the pathway each compound changes. The
publication answered it for DCF with an L1 penalty on the differences of all rate constants
between treated and untreated cells, scanned over the strength of the penalty. This chapter
answers it for all five compounds at once, with the compounds as the groups of a random effect
whose distribution is a spike and a slab: a compound leaves a rate constant exactly as it is, or
changes it by an amount drawn from a normal distribution. The probability of a change and the
spread of the changes are estimated from all compounds together. The code is `compounds.R`, on the
reduced model of [chapter 5](guide-profiles.html); [chapter 7](guide-nlme.html) introduces random
effects and their estimation by `em()`.

The second part of the chapter derives how `em()` integrates random effects whose deviations are
exactly zero unless the data need them: Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process random
effects.

## Data

Every compound comes with its own control: DCF on the blots and imaging of the first chapters, the
other four on a third set of blots with an untreated, stimulated control of their own. A condition
without a compound belongs to no group: `NA` in the column `compound`.

```{r compounddata}
```

```{r}
covariates(dataCompounds)
```

## Spike and slab

Write $\theta_k$ for the rate constant $k$ on the log scale, the same in every condition, and
$\eta_{ik}$ for its change by compound $i$; a condition with compound $i$ uses $\theta_k + \eta_{ik}$,
a condition without compound $\theta_k$. The spike-and-slab distribution
[@mitchell1988bayesian; @george1993variable] of a change is

$$p(\eta_{ik}) = (1 - \rho)\, \delta(\eta_{ik}) + \rho\, \mathcal{N}(\eta_{ik};\, 0, \tau^2),$$

a point mass at 0, the spike, with weight $1 - \rho$, and a normal slab of standard deviation $\tau$
with weight $\rho$. The changes are independent across compounds and rate constants; $\rho$ and
$\tau$ are shared by all. The likelihood of the fixed effects $\theta$ and the hyperparameters
$\rho, \tau$ integrates the changes out,

$$L(\theta, \rho, \tau) = \prod_i \int p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta_i)\, \prod_k p(\eta_{ik})\, d\eta_i ,$$

with $y_i$ the data of the conditions of compound $i$, times the likelihood of the conditions
without a compound. Each integral is a sum over the subsets $F$ of rate constants that compound $i$
changes: the spike sets $\eta_{ik} = 0$ for $k \notin F$, and the slab integrates the others,

$$\begin{aligned}
\int p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta_i)\, \prod_k p(\eta_{ik})\, d\eta_i
&= \sum_F \rho^{|F|} (1 - \rho)^{K - |F|} \\
&\quad \times \int p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta_F)\, \prod_{k \in F} \mathcal{N}(\eta_{ik};\, 0, \tau^2)\, d\eta_F ,
\end{aligned}$$

with $K$ the number of spike-and-slab random effects of a group, here the rate constants that may
change. `em(method = "focei")` approximates
$p(y_i \mid \theta, \eta_i)$ around the mode of $\eta_i$ as a Gaussian in $\eta_i$, with the
curvature $P_i$ of the data term, the Laplace approximation of [chapter 7](guide-nlme.html), so
every term of the sum is a Gaussian integral in closed form (section
[Approximate marginal](#approximate-marginal)). The posterior probability of the spike,
$p_0 = \Pr(\eta_{ik} = 0 \mid y)$, says how strongly the data of compound $i$ ask for a change of
rate constant $k$: a value near 0 is a change, a value near the prior probability of the spike,
$1 - \rho$, no evidence either way, and a value above it evidence against a change.

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = grouped}
rateConstants <- length(unique(readRDS("results/compounds.rds")$random$eta))
```

The data couple the changes of one compound through $P_i$, so the sum runs over all $2^K$ subsets.
Here every compound has `r if (grouped) rateConstants else "?"` rate constants that may change. The
sum leaves out the subsets the data make negligible (section [Spike and slab](#spike-and-slab-1)),
so its cost follows the changes the data leave undecided rather than $K$, and it is exact for every
compound here. Where it would exceed its budget, the coupling by the data is approximated by
expectation consistent [@opper2005expectation] (section [Expectation consistent](#expectation-consistent)).

The publication's L1 penalty $\lambda \sum |\eta_{ik}|$ is the mode of a Laplace distribution of the
changes [@tibshirani1996regression]: it sets small changes to exactly 0, with a strength $\lambda$
chosen by a scan, and gives no probability of a change.

## Model

The reduced model of [chapter 5](guide-profiles.html) with second derivatives, which `em()` uses,
and each condition at rest at its own steady state:

```{r compoundmodel, eval = FALSE}
```

`insert()` with an effect formula writes the change: `x ~ 1 + (1 | gr(compound, dist =
spikeSlab()))` replaces the rate constant `x` by its fixed effect plus a random effect of the
compound. The scales and offsets of the third set of blots are parameters of their own.

```{r compoundeffects, eval = FALSE}
```

## Fit

`em()` estimates the fixed effects, the modes of the changes and $\rho$ and $\tau$ together.
`compounds.R` runs it from 200 starts, the reduced model at its optimum with the changes at 0 and
199 starts around it; a start whose fit fails is drawn again. The fits ran as 100 tasks
of two on a SLURM cluster, with `msem(which = )` and `distributedComputing()`
([chapter 11](guide-remote-computing.html)):

```{r compoundfit, eval = FALSE}
```

The best fit is saved with a table of all starts:

```{r compoundsave, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !grouped}
cat("> Results pending: `results/compounds.rds` of the project is written by `compounds.R`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = grouped}
fit <- readRDS("results/compounds.rds")
c(value = fit$value, converged = fit$converged, iterations = fit$iterations)
fit$argument[c("prob_compound", "tau_compound")]
fit$coupling
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = grouped}
couplingText <- switch(fit$coupling %||% "none",
  expectationConsistent = "expectation consistent",
  none = "none: every compound is integrated exactly")
```

`value` is $-2 \log L$ of the approximate marginal, `iterations` the steps of the one trust region
in which the fixed effects and the hyperparameters move. `coupling` names the integral over the
changes that the data couple, here `r if (grouped) couplingText`.

## Multistart

The objective of the compounds has local optima like that of any fit, and at a start far from the
optimum the resting state may not be stable: NFκB oscillates there. `pSSCompounds` returns that
root, and the term of `constraintStability()` rises with it, as in [chapter 1](guide-model.html).
`msem()` draws a start again where its fit fails, for instance where expectation consistent does
not converge. The table `$multistart` of the saved fit has a row per
start: its `value`, whether it `converged`, its `iterations`, the attempts it took (`tries`), and
the `error` of a start that failed every attempt. The waterfall shows the best 100 starts sorted by
$-2 \log L$; starts on one plateau ended in the same optimum.

```{r, include = FALSE}
multistart <- grouped && is.data.frame(fit$multistart)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !multistart}
cat("> Multistart pending: the saved fit holds no table of starts; `compounds.R` writes it to `$multistart`.\n")
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.5, eval = multistart}
plotValues(fit, rank(value, ties.method = "first") <= 100)
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = multistart}
ms <- fit$multistart
best <- min(ms$value, na.rm = TRUE)
multistartText <- sprintf(
  "Of the %d starts, %d end within 1 of the best -2 log L, %d did not converge and %d failed.",
  nrow(ms), sum(ms$value < best + 1, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!ms$converged & !is.na(ms$value)),
  sum(is.na(ms$value)))
retriedText <- if (is.null(ms$tries) || !any(ms$tries > 1)) "" else
  sprintf("%d of the starts were drawn again, %d times in all.", sum(ms$tries > 1), sum(ms$tries - 1))
```

`r if (multistart) multistartText` `r if (multistart) retriedText`

## Changes

The changes with a posterior probability of the spike below 0.05, by compound, with their modes on
the log scale:

```{r, eval = grouped}
changes <- fit$random[fit$random$p0 < 0.05, c("group", "eta", "mode", "se", "p0")]
changes <- changes[order(changes$group, changes$p0), ]
rownames(changes) <- NULL
changes
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = grouped}
compounds <- sort(unique(fit$random$group))
rates <- unique(fit$random$eta)
counts <- table(factor(changes$group, levels = compounds))
others <- setdiff(compounds, "DCF")
changesText <- sprintf(
  "DCF changes %d of the %d rate constants, %s. The probability of a change is %.2f, and a change has a spread of %.2f on the log scale, a factor of about %.1f.",
  counts[["DCF"]], length(rates), enumerate(sprintf("%s %d", others, counts[others])),
  fit$argument[["prob_compound"]], fit$argument[["tau_compound"]], exp(fit$argument[["tau_compound"]]))
```

`r if (grouped) changesText`

```{r, fig.height = 5.5, eval = grouped}
shown <- fit$random
shown$eta <- factor(shown$eta, levels = unique(shown$eta))
shown$evidence <- -log10(pmax(shown$p0, 1e-6))
ggplot2::ggplot(shown, ggplot2::aes(group, eta)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(ggplot2::aes(fill = mode, alpha = evidence), colour = "white") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = shown[shown$p0 < 0.05, ], ggplot2::aes(shape = "p0 < 0.05"),
                      size = 1.8, fill = "white") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b") +
  ggplot2::scale_alpha(range = c(0.1, 1), limits = c(0, 6), breaks = 1:3,
                       labels = c("1, p0 = 0.1", "2, p0 = 0.01", "3, p0 = 0.001"),
                       guide = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = "grey30"))) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = 21) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "change [log]", alpha = "evidence, -log10 p0", shape = NULL) +
  theme_dMod()
```

Every tile is one compound and one rate constant, the random effect $\eta_{ik}$; the rate constants
follow the pathway, from IKK at the top to A20 at the bottom. The colour of a tile is the mode of
the change on the log scale, that of the most probable structure: red an increase, blue a decrease,
white no change, which is the mode wherever the spike is more probable than the slab. A mode of
$-0.7$ halves the rate constant. The opacity of a tile is the evidence for a change,
$-\log_{10} p_0$, with $p_0$ the posterior probability of the spike, that is of no change at all:
1 is $p_0 = 0.1$, 2 is $p_0 = 0.01$, 3 is $p_0 = 0.001$, and from 6 on, $p_0$ below $10^{-6}$, the
tile has its full colour. A pale tile is either a small change or a rate constant that the data of
the compound leave where it is or say nothing about, with $p_0$ near or above the prior probability
of the spike, $1 - \rho$. The circle tells the two apart: it marks the tiles with $p_0 < 0.05$, the
changes of the table above. A coloured tile without a circle is a change more probable than none,
but with $p_0$ between 0.05 and 0.5.

## Comparison with the publication

The publication selected the changes of DCF by an L1 penalty on the full model, in its
supplement; it found seven rate constants changed. The table lists them with every change the spike
and slab finds for DCF, with the reaction each rate constant belongs to:

```{r, eval = grouped}
publication <- c("act_Ikb_by_Ikk", "act_Ikk_by_TNF", "act_pIkk", "degrad_mIkb",
                 "prod_mIkb_by_nNfk", "shuttle_RnaA20", "trigger_iIkk")
dcf <- fit$random[fit$random$group == "DCF", c("eta", "mode", "p0")]
dcf <- dcf[dcf$eta %in% publication | dcf$p0 < 0.05, ]
dcf$publication <- dcf$eta %in% publication
dcf$spikeSlab <- dcf$p0 < 0.05
# the reaction of a rate constant: of those whose rate uses it, the one with the fewest symbols
dcf$reaction <- vapply(dcf$eta, function(k) {
  symbols <- lapply(reactionsReduced$rates, function(r) all.vars(str2lang(r)))
  uses <- which(vapply(symbols, function(s) k %in% s, TRUE))
  reactionsReduced$description[uses[which.min(lengths(symbols[uses]))]]
}, "")
dcf <- dcf[order(!dcf$publication, !dcf$spikeSlab, dcf$p0), ]
yes <- function(x) ifelse(x, "yes", "no")
knitr::kable(data.frame(dcf$eta, yes(dcf$publication), yes(dcf$spikeSlab), round(dcf$mode, 2),
                        formatC(dcf$p0, format = "g", digits = 2), dcf$reaction),
             row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("rate constant", "publication", "spike and slab",
                                               "mode", "$p_0$", "reaction"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = grouped}
foundDCF <- dcf$eta[dcf$publication & dcf$spikeSlab]
missedDCF <- dcf[dcf$publication & !dcf$spikeSlab, ]
addedDCF <- dcf$eta[!dcf$publication & dcf$spikeSlab]
dcfText <- paste0(
  sprintf("Of the seven, the spike and slab finds %d: %s. ", length(foundDCF), enumerate(code(foundDCF))),
  if (nrow(missedDCF)) sprintf("It leaves %s at the population value, %s. ",
                              enumerate(code(missedDCF$eta)),
                              enumerate(sprintf("$p_0 = %.2g$", missedDCF$p0))),
  if (length(addedDCF)) sprintf("It adds %d: %s.", length(addedDCF), enumerate(code(addedDCF)))
  else "It adds none.")
perCompound <- vapply(others, function(g) {
  k <- changes$eta[changes$group == g]
  if (!length(k)) return(sprintf("none for %s", g))
  sprintf("%d for %s (%s)", length(k), g, enumerate(code(k)))
}, "")
othersText <- sprintf("The spike and slab finds %s.", enumerate(perCompound))
```

`r if (grouped) dcfText`

For AMD, APAP, FIAU and XIM the publication estimated no changes; it predicted A20 for them under
two scenarios. `r if (grouped) othersText`

The two analyses differ in three respects. The model: the reduced model of
[chapter 5](guide-profiles.html) has fewer processes than the full model of the publication; a
process the reduction made fast or removed cannot change, and a change of the full model may show
on a neighbouring rate constant of the reduced one. The criterion: the L1 scan selects the changes
at one strength of the penalty, the spike and slab by the posterior probability of no change, with
$\rho$ and $\tau$ estimated from all five compounds, so that the data of each compound inform the
prior of the others through these two numbers. And the threshold: $p_0 < 0.05$ is a choice;
`fit$random` holds $p_0$ for every compound and rate constant, and with it the reading at any other
threshold.

## The full model

The model is the one difference the reduced model adds to the comparison. `compoundsFull.R` takes
the full model of [chapter 1](guide-model.html), on which the publication ran its L1 scan, with a
spike-and-slab random effect over the compounds on every rate constant but the gauge, and the same
data:

```{r, include = FALSE}
full <- file.exists(file.path(project, "results", "compoundsFull.rds"))
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018/compoundsFull.R")
```

```{r fullcompoundeffects, eval = FALSE}
```

The full model has directions the data leave flat ([chapter 5](guide-profiles.html)); the slab
regularises the changes, not the population values, which keep the weak prior of `model.R`, as in
the fits of the publication:

```{r fullprior, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !full}
cat("> Results pending: `results/compoundsFull.rds` of the project is written by `compoundsFull.R`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = full}
fitFull <- readRDS(file.path(project, "results", "compoundsFull.rds"))
dcfFull <- fitFull$random[fitFull$random$group == "DCF", c("eta", "mode", "p0")]
rows <- union(publication, union(dcf$eta[dcf$spikeSlab], dcfFull$eta[dcfFull$p0 < 0.05]))
knitr::kable(data.frame(rows, yes(rows %in% publication), yes(rows %in% dcf$eta[dcf$spikeSlab]),
                        yes(rows %in% dcfFull$eta[dcfFull$p0 < 0.05])),
             col.names = c("rate constant", "publication", "reduced model", "full model"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = full}
selFull <- dcfFull$eta[dcfFull$p0 < 0.05]
core <- Reduce(intersect, list(publication, dcf$eta[dcf$spikeSlab], selFull))
dropped <- dcfFull[dcfFull$eta %in% setdiff(publication, selFull), ]
both <- intersect(dcf$eta[dcf$spikeSlab], selFull)
flips <- both[sign(dcf$mode[match(both, dcf$eta)]) != sign(dcfFull$mode[match(both, dcfFull$eta)])]
fullText <- paste0(
  sprintf("All three analyses change %s. On the full model the spike and slab leaves %s at the population value, with %s",
          enumerate(code(core)), enumerate(code(dropped$eta)), enumerate(sprintf("$p_0 = %.2f$", dropped$p0))),
  if (length(flips)) sprintf(", and it changes %s in the direction opposite to the reduced model.", enumerate(code(flips)))
  else ".")
```

`r if (full) fullText`

On the full model, which rate constants change under DCF rests on the directions the data leave
flat ([chapter 5](guide-profiles.html)): there the weak prior of the population values, not the
data, decides between structures that fit equally well, and a different prior width moves the
selection between neighbouring rate constants. The reduced model keeps only what the data
determine, and its changes are the reading to rely on. The comparison also shows that the
selection of the publication on the full model stands on the same flat directions.

Which method to trust where the model is identifiable follows from how the two select. A
likelihood-ratio test per rate constant does not work here: with 21 to 33 rate constants per
compound there are $2^{21}$ to $2^{33}$ structures, the test of one rate depends on which others
are free, and coupled rates give a different answer for every order. Both methods replace that
search. The L1 penalty shrinks every selected change towards 0 by the same amount and pays for it
by selecting further small changes; among rate constants the data tie together it keeps one, and
which one is not stable, the condition under which the lasso finds the right set fails for such
correlations. The spike and slab separates the decision from the size: a change is either exactly 0
or drawn from the slab, whose spread $\tau$ shrinks a selected change only little, and the exact
sum over the subsets weighs every structure by its marginal likelihood, the all-subsets comparison
done in one integral, with $\rho$ and $\tau$ estimated by maximum likelihood instead of a strength
set by hand. Where the data cannot tell coupled rates apart, the probability spreads over the
structures that explain the data equally well, and $p_0$ of each stays in between. Within the
Laplace approximation of the data term, the spike and slab is the more reliable reading on an
identifiable model; on the full model neither method can decide what the data leave flat.

## Sparse random effects

`gr(group, dist = )` in an effect formula sets the distribution of the random effects of a term.
Besides `normal()`, three distributions have deviations that are exactly zero unless the data need
them:

| distribution | a deviation $\eta$ of a group | hyperparameters |
|---|---|---|
| `laplace()` | density $\tfrac{\lambda}{2} e^{-\lambda \lvert \eta \rvert}$ | strength `lambda_<grouping>` |
| `spikeSlab()` | $0$ with probability $1 - \rho$, else from $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ | `prob_<grouping>`, `tau_<grouping>` |
| `dirichletProcess()` | the value of its cluster: $0$ for the cluster of the population value, else one draw from $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ per cluster | `concentration_<grouping>`, `tau_<grouping>` |

The hyperparameters are shared by all symbols of a term, numbered `_1`, `_2`, ... where a grouping
has several such terms, and estimated with the fixed effects unless given, as in
`laplace(lambda = 2)`. A Laplace deviation has its mode at exactly zero unless the data pull it
away, so the fit sorts shared from group-specific parameters, with one strength $\lambda$ per term
estimated from all its deviations. A spike-and-slab deviation is zero with a probability, which the
fit reports per group. Under the Dirichlet process the groups of a symbol share deviations: they
form clusters with the population value, the section
[Dirichlet-process random effects](#dirichlet-process-random-effects) treats them. Normal and sparse
random effects of one grouping may be combined; `em(method = "focei")` fits all of them,
Dirichlet-process ones also `method = "saem"`.

## Approximate marginal

Write $D_i(\eta_i)$ for the data $-2 \log L$ of group $i$ at its random effects $\eta_i$, summed
over its conditions, and split the random effects of a group into the normal coordinates $N$ and
the sparse ones $S$ (Laplace, spike and slab, Dirichlet process).

### Joint mode

`em()` first finds the joint mode $\hat\eta$ of all random effects, minimising

$$\begin{aligned}
\Phi(\eta) = {} & \sum_i \Bigl[ D_i(\eta_i) + \eta_{iN}^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_{iN} \Bigr] \\
& + \sum_{\text{Laplace}} 2 \lambda \lvert \eta \rvert
+ \sum_{\text{spike and slab, Dirichlet}} \frac{\eta^2}{\tau^2} :
\end{aligned}$$

the data, the normal prior, the L1 penalty of the Laplace coordinates, and for spike-and-slab and
Dirichlet-process coordinates the slab alone. $\Phi$ is a sum over the groups, whose random effects
enter only their own conditions, so each group is minimised on its own: by `trustL1()`
([chapter 4](guide-optimization.html)) where it has Laplace coordinates, by `trust()` otherwise.
The model Hessian is Gauss-Newton plus a BFGS correction from the points that lowered $\Phi$: where
the residuals stay large, Gauss-Newton alone overestimates the curvature and converges only
linearly. A random effect that reaches no data of its group, along the transformations, the ODE
and the observables, rests at 0 (section [Reported structure](#reported-structure)). This mode is
smooth in the parameters, so the marginal does not jump where the most probable structure changes.
Every evaluation starts from the modes of the last accepted point, moved to first order along the
step (section [Exact gradient](#exact-gradient)), and solves to the tolerances of the outer trust
region, $10^{-10}$ where none are given. The problem of a group may have several local minima, and
the Laplace approximation belongs to the lowest, which outweighs one higher by $e^{\Delta\Phi / 2}$.
So a group starts from the lowest of these modes and of the minima found at its last four distinct
accepted points; a step does not fall into a higher minimum while a lower one is known. At the
start of the fit and every 25 accepted steps the search runs for every group also from 0 and from
two starts around its modes, each random effect moved by its slab standard deviation, and the
lowest minimum joins those known; the moves are fixed numbers, so that `em()` draws no random
numbers.

### Normal coordinates

Around the mode the data term is expanded to second order, with the gradient $\nabla D_i$ and the
Gauss-Newton curvature $H_i$ of the data term alone in the random effects; $H_{NN}$ is its normal
block plus the prior precision $2 \Omega^{-1}$, the curvature $H_i$ of
[chapter 7](guide-nlme.html#laplace-approximation) in the normal coordinates. At the mode the
gradient of the data term and the normal prior vanishes in the normal coordinates, so on the
quadratic model they integrate out exactly. They leave the volume $\log \lvert H_{NN}/2 \rvert$, as
in FOCEI, and for the sparse coordinates the Schur complement

$$\tilde H_i = H_{SS} - H_{SN} H_{NN}^{-1} H_{NS},$$

so that the data term on the sparse coordinates is, up to a constant, the Gaussian
$\exp(-\tfrac12 \eta_{iS}^\top P_i\, \eta_{iS} + b_i^\top \eta_{iS})$ with

$$P_i = \tilde H_i / 2, \qquad b_i = \tfrac12 \bigl( \tilde H_i\, \hat\eta_{iS} - \nabla_S D_i \bigr)$$

per group, $\nabla_S D_i$ the gradient of the data term in the sparse coordinates. Unlike
$P_i = H_i/2$ of chapter 7, $P_i$ holds no prior: the prior of the sparse coordinates is not
Gaussian and enters the integral $I$ below exactly. $P_i$ may be singular, where the data of a
group do not see a coordinate or a combination of coordinates; the integral needs no inverse of
it.

### Value

The expansion gives

$$\begin{aligned}
-2 \log L \approx {} & \sum_i \Bigl[ D_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_{NN}/2 \rvert
+ \tfrac12 \hat\eta_{iS}^\top \tilde H_i\, \hat\eta_{iS} - \nabla_S D_i^\top \hat\eta_{iS} \\
& \qquad + \hat\eta_{iN}^\top \Omega^{-1} \hat\eta_{iN} \Bigr]
+ G \log \lvert \Omega \rvert - 2 \log I + D_0 ,
\end{aligned}$$

with $D_0$ the $-2 \log L$ of the conditions without random effects and of the other terms of the
objective, such as priors, and

$$I = \int \prod_i \exp\Bigl( -\tfrac12\, \eta_{iS}^\top P_i\, \eta_{iS} + b_i^\top \eta_{iS} \Bigr)\,
p(\eta_S)\, d\eta_S$$

over the sparse coordinates of all groups, $p$ their prior. Without sparse coordinates this is the
FOCEI value of [chapter 7](guide-nlme.html). Every structure, a subset of spike coordinates or a
partition into clusters, is a Gaussian integral under the expansion. $I$ is a product of
one-dimensional integrals only where every $P_i$ is diagonal and the prior a product over the
coordinates. The Laplace and spike-and-slab priors are products over the groups, the Dirichlet
process couples the groups of a symbol, and the data couple the coordinates of a group through the
off-diagonal entries of $P_i$.

## Factor integrals

$I$ is evaluated in factors, each integrated exactly:

- every Laplace symbol, over all groups, a product of one-dimensional integrals;
- every Dirichlet-process symbol, its coordinates of all groups jointly;
- the spike-and-slab symbols of a group jointly, within a budget of terms; beyond it, each alone.

A factor is integrated against an exponential tilt $\exp(h^\top \eta - \tfrac12 \eta^\top T \eta)$:
its Gaussian part with $T = P_{ff}$ in the uncoupled case, a diagonal $T$ under expectation
consistent below. A tilt with $T = 0$, a coordinate the data do not see, is no special
case. With $\log Z(h, T)$ the log integral, Fisher's identity gives

$$\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial h} = \mathbb{E}\, \eta, \qquad
\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial T} = -\tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}\, \eta \eta^\top,$$

and the derivative in a hyperparameter is the posterior expectation of the derivative of the log
prior.

### Laplace

A Laplace coordinate against the tilt $(h, t)$, $t > 0$, integrates in closed form,

$$\begin{aligned}
Z(h, t, \lambda) &= \int \frac{\lambda}{2} e^{-\lambda \lvert \eta \rvert}\, e^{h \eta - t \eta^2 / 2}\, d\eta \\
&= \frac{\lambda}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2t}}\,
\bigl[ \operatorname{erfcx}(x_+) + \operatorname{erfcx}(x_-) \bigr], \qquad
x_\pm = \frac{\lambda \mp h}{\sqrt{2t}},
\end{aligned}$$

the two terms the halves $\eta > 0$ and $\eta < 0$, with $\operatorname{erfcx}(x) = e^{x^2}
\operatorname{erfc}(x)$ the scaled complementary error function. It stays finite where
$\operatorname{erfc}$ underflows: $\log \operatorname{erfcx}$ comes from the logarithm of the normal
distribution function up to $x = 10$ and from its asymptotic series beyond. Each half is a
truncated normal; its moments $\mathbb{E}\, u^k$ of $u = \eta \sqrt t$ follow from the recurrence
$I_k + \alpha I_{k-1} = (k-1) I_{k-2}$ of $I_k = \int_0^\infty u^k e^{-u^2/2 - \alpha u}\, du$,
forward for small $\alpha = \sqrt{2}\, x_\pm$ and by its continued fraction for the ratios
$I_k / I_{k-1}$ beyond, so that they stay accurate as $t \to 0$, where a half tends to an
exponential distribution. $\mathbb{E}\, \lvert \eta \rvert = 1/\lambda - \partial \log Z / \partial
\lambda$.

### Spike and slab

The spike-and-slab coordinates of a group against the tilt $(h, T)$ integrate as a sum over the
subsets $F$ of coordinates in the slab. With the covariance
$V_F = (T_{FF} + \tau^{-2} \mathbb{1})^{-1}$ of the slab coordinates given $F$,

$$Z = \sum_F \rho^{|F|} (1 - \rho)^{K - |F|}\,
\frac{\lvert V_F \rvert^{1/2}}{\tau^{|F|}}\,
\exp\bigl( \tfrac12 h_F^\top V_F\, h_F \bigr) ,$$

$2^K$ terms for the $K$ coordinates of the factor. A term is the Gaussian integral over the slab
coordinates with the others at 0; the factors $2\pi$ of the slab density and of the integral
cancel. The posterior probability $\Pr(F \mid y)$ of a subset is its term divided by $Z$; given
the subset, $\eta_F$ is normal with mean $\mu_F = V_F\, h_F$ and covariance $V_F$, and the other
coordinates are 0. The posterior is the mixture of these normals, with the moments

$$\begin{aligned}
1 - p_{0k} &= \sum_{F \ni k} \Pr(F \mid y), \\
\mathbb{E}\, \eta &= \sum_F \Pr(F \mid y)\, \mu_F, \\
\mathbb{E}\, \eta \eta^\top &= \sum_F \Pr(F \mid y) \bigl( V_F + \mu_F \mu_F^\top \bigr),
\end{aligned}$$

$\mu_F$ and $V_F$ filled with zeros outside $F$: the probability of coordinate $k$ to be in the
slab, the posterior mean, and the second moment, whose diagonal $\mathbb{E}\, \eta_k^2$ comes from
the slab alone. The covariance is full within the factor. Fisher's identity gives the derivatives
in the hyperparameters, summed over the coordinates that share them,

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial \rho} &= \sum_k \Bigl( \frac{1 - p_{0k}}{\rho} - \frac{p_{0k}}{1 - \rho} \Bigr), \\
\frac{\partial \log Z}{\partial \tau} &= \sum_k \Bigl( -\frac{1 - p_{0k}}{\tau} + \frac{\mathbb{E}\, \eta_k^2}{\tau^3} \Bigr) .
\end{aligned}$$

The sum runs as a depth-first search over the coordinates, each in or out of the slab. With $L$
the Cholesky factor of $V_F^{-1}$, including a coordinate adds one row to $W = L^{-1}$, so that a
term costs $O(K^2)$ and not $O(K^3)$. Since $V_F = W^\top W$ is the sum of the outer products of the
rows of $W$, and a row depends only on the coordinates before it, every included coordinate adds
its row's outer product times the weight of all terms below it; the means $\mu_F$ of the terms and
these rows enter the second moment in blocks, by a symmetric rank-$k$ update. A subtree is left out
where a bound on its terms falls below $e^{-40}$ of the largest term found, at most $2^K e^{-40}$
of $Z$: $h_F^\top V_F h_F$ grows with $F$, so it is at most that of the subset of the coordinates in
the slab and those still open, and every later diagonal entry of $L$ is at least the conditional
precision of its coordinate given that subset. The branch with the larger bound goes first, so the
largest terms are found early; where the data decide most coordinates, few terms remain.

A single coordinate needs only $t > -\tau^{-2}$. The search visits at most $2^{24}$ nodes, a few
seconds; a group that would need more goes to expectation consistent, every spike-and-slab
coordinate a factor of its own.

### Clusters

A Dirichlet-process symbol integrates by a sum over the partitions of its groups, a recursion over
subsets given in the section [Partition sum](#partition-sum).

## Expectation consistent

The groups are integrated one by one where no Dirichlet-process symbol joins them, a group whose
factors the data do not couple exactly. The factors are coupled where the data of a group link
coordinates of different factors, the off-diagonal blocks $P_{ff'}$ of the precision between
factors $f$ and $f'$. There, and where the joint spike-and-slab sum would exceed its budget, the
integral is the expectation-consistent approximation of Opper and Winther [@opper2005expectation]. Write the integrand of $I$ as the product of the prior $p$
of the factors and the Gaussian coupling $\mathcal{G}(\eta) = \prod_i \exp(-\tfrac12 \eta_i^\top
P_i \eta_i + b_i^\top \eta_i)$, and look at it in two tractable ways, with the statistics
$\phi(\eta) = (\eta_k, -\eta_k^2/2)_k$ of every coordinate:

- $q \propto p\, e^{\lambda^\top \phi}$, every factor exact against a diagonal cavity $\lambda$;
- $r \propto \mathcal{G}\, e^{\gamma^\top \phi}$, the coupling exact under diagonal sites $\gamma$,
  a Gaussian of precision $P_i + \operatorname{diag}(\gamma_t)$ per group.

With $A_q(\lambda) = \log \int p\, e^{\lambda^\top \phi}$, $A_r(\gamma) = \log \int \mathcal{G}\,
e^{\gamma^\top \phi}$ and $A_s(\nu) = \log \int e^{\nu^\top \phi}$ the log integrals, a product of
one-dimensional Gaussians for $A_s$,

$$\log I \;\approx\; A_q(\lambda) + A_r(\gamma) - A_s(\nu), \qquad \nu = \lambda + \gamma,$$

at a point where $q$, $r$ and $e^{\nu^\top \phi}$ have the same mean and variance in every
coordinate. The cavity is the effective field of the other factors on one factor, solved
self-consistently with its fluctuations. The result is exact without coupling and for Gaussian
factors; it is not a bound.

The fixed point is found by a double loop that converges whatever the coupling [@heskes2005approximate].
Its outer step sets $\nu$ to the natural parameters of the current marginals, $\nu_t = 1 /
\operatorname{Var}\, \eta_k$ and $\nu_h = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_k / \operatorname{Var}\, \eta_k$. The
inner loop minimises

$$\Psi_\nu(\lambda) = A_q(\lambda) + A_r(\nu - \lambda),$$

convex in $\lambda$ as the sum of two log integrals, whose gradient $\mathbb{E}_q \phi -
\mathbb{E}_r \phi$ vanishes where the moments of $q$ and $r$ match. Newton steps on the Hessian
$\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi$ with a backtracking line search on $\Psi$
converge quadratically; the third and fourth moments of the factors enter $\operatorname{Cov}_q
\phi$, and for a Dirichlet-process symbol of up to ten groups also its moments between groups, so
that the step solves all coordinates jointly. The cavity is the variable, so no cavity precision is
formed as a difference $1 / \operatorname{Var}_r \eta_k - \gamma_{t,k}$, and a site precision may be
negative. A step is confined to the domains of the integrals: the Gaussian part positive definite,
tested by a Cholesky factor of its Jacobi-scaled precision, $\lambda_t > -\tau^{-2}$ for a slab
coordinate, $\lambda_t > 0$ for a Laplace coordinate, and $\tau^{-2} + \sum_g \min(\lambda_{t,g}, 0)
> 0$ for a Dirichlet-process symbol. Each evaluation starts from the sites of the last accepted
point.

That outer step converges linearly, slowly where the data tie coordinates closely. The outer loop
therefore takes Newton steps on the condition $\mathbb{E}_q \phi(\lambda^*(\nu)) = \mathbb{E}_s
\phi(\nu)$, with $s \propto e^{\nu^\top \phi}$ and $\lambda^*(\nu)$ the solution of the inner loop. Differentiating its condition
gives $\mathrm{d}\lambda^* = (\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi)^{-1}
\operatorname{Cov}_r \phi\; \mathrm{d}\nu$, so the Jacobian is

$$\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi\, (\operatorname{Cov}_q \phi + \operatorname{Cov}_r \phi)^{-1}
\operatorname{Cov}_r \phi - \operatorname{Cov}_s \phi ,$$

solved after scaling its rows and columns, since a coordinate the data pin at 0 has second moments
many orders below the others. The cavities move with $\mathrm{d}\lambda^*$, which starts the next
inner loop near its solution. A Newton step that does not lower the largest mismatch of the moments
gives way to the fixed-point step from the iterate before it, and the next ten rounds take
fixed-point steps.

The inner loop ends where the means match to $10^{-10}$ standard deviations and the variances to
$10^{-10}$ relative, or, within $10^{-4}$, where a Newton step no longer lowers $\Psi$; the outer one
where the marginals of $r$ match the Gaussians of $\nu$ to $10^{-10}$ in the same units, or, within
$10^{-4}$, where the mismatch stops falling for twenty rounds. The second criterion is the rounding of an ill-conditioned Gaussian part, where
the data tie coordinates closely. A point at which the double loop does not converge is a failed
evaluation of the trust region, which shrinks its radius and tries a shorter step. `fit$coupling`
is `"expectationConsistent"` where a group needed it, and `NULL` where every group is exact.

## Exact gradient

At the fixed point the value is stationary in the sites and cavities, so the derivatives of
$\log I$ in $b$, $P$ and the hyperparameters hold them fixed; for exact factors these are Fisher's
identity:

$$\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial b_i} = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}, \qquad
\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial P_i} = -\tfrac12 \bigl( \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}\, \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS}^\top + \Sigma_i \bigr),$$

with $\Sigma_i$ the posterior covariance of the sparse coordinates of group $i$. For exact factors
$\mathbb{E}$ and $\Sigma_i$ are those of the posterior, block diagonal over the factors; under
expectation consistent $\mathbb{E}$ is $\mathbb{E}_r$ and $\Sigma_i$ the covariance of $r$, full
within the group. The derivative in a hyperparameter is the expectation of the derivative of its
log prior under the factors, at the cavity under expectation consistent: Fisher's identity per
factor.

Through $b_i = \tfrac12 (\tilde H_i \hat\eta_{iS} - \nabla_S D_i)$ and $P_i = \tilde H_i / 2$ these
give, with $\delta_i = \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{iS} - \hat\eta_{iS}$, the derivatives of $-2 \log L$ in
$\nabla_S D_i$, $\tilde H_i$ and the mode,

$$\delta_i, \qquad \tfrac12 \bigl( \delta_i \delta_i^\top + \Sigma_i \bigr), \qquad
-\tilde H_i\, \delta_i - \nabla_S D_i ,$$

and through the Schur complement those in $H_i$ and $\Omega$. From there the chain needs
$\partial \nabla D_i / \partial \psi$ from the exact Hessian of the data term,
$\partial H_i / \partial \psi$ and $\partial H_i / \partial \eta$ from second derivatives of the
prediction and the error model, as for the volume term of FOCEI in [chapter 7](guide-nlme.html),
and the shift of the mode.

The mode moves with the parameters $\psi$ in its free coordinates: the normal ones, the
spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process ones, whose inner objective has the slab alone, and the
Laplace coordinates away from zero; those at zero stay there. With $W$ the matrix whose columns
select the free coordinates, $\eta = W \xi$, the stationarity of the inner objective,
$W^\top (\nabla_\eta \Phi + \text{subgradient}) = 0$, gives

$$\frac{d \xi}{d \psi} = -\bigl( W^\top \nabla^2_\eta \Phi\, W \bigr)^{-1} W^\top \nabla^2_{\eta \psi} \Phi .$$

The curvature of the inner objective is block diagonal by groups, so the shift of a group is its
own. The same shift with the derivative of the subgradient in a hyperparameter, $2 \operatorname{sign}
\eta$ in $\lambda$ and $-4 \eta / \tau^3$ in $\tau$, gives the derivatives in $\lambda$ and $\tau$
through the mode; $\rho$ and the concentration $\alpha$ do not enter the inner objective and do not
move it. The shift also gives the first-order start of the inner modes at the next trial point. The
gradient is exact for the approximate marginal.

## Hyperparameters

### E-step

`em()` does not alternate E- and M-steps: every evaluation of the approximate marginal is an
E-step, and the M-steps below set the curvature of the hyperparameters in the joint trust region.
[Chapter 7](guide-nlme.html#em-algorithm) derives EM in general; for the spike and slab the E-step
forms the posterior moments of the deviations that the objective of $\rho$ and $\tau$ needs. This
chapter writes that objective on the scale of $-2 \log L$, as $-2Q$ with $Q$ the expected
complete-data log-density of chapter 7, and minimises it.

With the indicator $z_{ik}$, 1 for a deviation in the slab and 0 for one in the spike, the
complete data are $(\eta, z)$, and their $-2 \log$ prior, summed over the groups $i$ and the
symbols $k$ of a term, is up to terms free of $\rho$ and $\tau$

$$\begin{aligned}
-2 \log p(\eta, z \mid \rho, \tau) = \sum_{i,k} \Bigl[ & -2 z_{ik} \log \rho - 2 (1 - z_{ik}) \log (1 - \rho) \\
& + z_{ik} \Bigl( 2 \log \tau + \frac{\eta_{ik}^2}{\tau^2} \Bigr) \Bigr] .
\end{aligned}$$

Its posterior expectation is the complete-data objective of the M-steps,

$$\begin{aligned}
-2Q(\rho, \tau) = {} & -2 \bar n \log \rho - 2 (n - \bar n) \log (1 - \rho) \\
& + 2 \bar n \log \tau + \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^2} ,
\end{aligned}$$

$n$ the number of deviations of the term. It depends on the data only through two expected
sufficient statistics, the expected number $\bar n$ of deviations in the slab and the expected sum
of their squares $v^2$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\bar n &= \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, z_{ik} = \sum_{i,k} (1 - p_{0,ik}), \\
\mathbb{E} \sum v^2 &= \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, z_{ik} \eta_{ik}^2 = \sum_{i,k} \mathbb{E}\, \eta_{ik}^2 ,
\end{aligned}$$

the last since $\eta_{ik} = 0$ wherever $z_{ik} = 0$.

The expectations are taken under the posterior of the approximate marginal. For group $i$ it is
the quadratic model of the data term at the joint mode, with the Gauss-Newton curvature and the
normal coordinates integrated out (section [Normal coordinates](#normal-coordinates)), times the
exact prior,

$$p(\eta_{iS} \mid y_i) \propto \exp\Bigl( -\tfrac12 (\eta_{iS} - m_i)^\top P_i\, (\eta_{iS} - m_i) \Bigr)
\prod_k p(\eta_{ik}) ,$$

and the groups are independent under it. The spike-and-slab symbols of a group form one factor,
the subset sum of section [Spike and slab](#spike-and-slab-1); without coupled sparse coordinates
it is integrated on $(P_i, m_i)$ and gives the moments of this posterior exactly. Under expectation
consistent every spike-and-slab coordinate is a factor alone, integrated on a one-dimensional Gaussian
of precision $a$ and centre $m$, a sum of two terms. Given a deviation, the slab has the posterior
variance $V$, the $V_F$ of one coordinate, and the posterior mean $\mu$,

$$V = \frac{1}{a + \tau^{-2}}, \qquad \mu = V a\, m .$$

The probability of a deviation is the inverse logit of the posterior log odds of slab and spike,

$$1 - p_0 = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} \Bigl( \operatorname{logit} \rho + \frac{\mu^2}{2 V}
+ \tfrac12 \log \frac{V}{\tau^2} \Bigr) :$$

the prior log odds, the gain of the exponent at the slab mean over the spike at 0, and the log
ratio of the posterior to the prior width of the slab. The moments are those of the mixture of the
spike and the slab,

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\, \eta &= (1 - p_0)\, \mu, \\
\mathbb{E}\, \eta^2 &= (1 - p_0)\, (\mu^2 + V), \\
\operatorname{Var} \eta &= \mathbb{E}\, \eta^2 - (\mathbb{E}\, \eta)^2 .
\end{aligned}$$

Under expectation consistent every coordinate has its cavity, $a = a^c_{ik}$ and $m = m^c_{ik}$
(section [Expectation consistent](#expectation-consistent)). $p_0$, $\mathbb{E}\, \eta$ and
$\mathbb{E}\, \eta^2$ are those of $q$, whose means and variances equal those of $r$ at the fixed
point, and $\Sigma_i = (P_i + \operatorname{diag} \Lambda_i)^{-1}$ is the covariance of $r$.

Given its sparse coordinates, the normal coordinates of a group are normal on the expansion,

$$\begin{aligned}
\eta_{iN} \mid \eta_{iS} &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl( \hat\eta_{iN} - R_i\, (\eta_{iS} - \hat\eta_{iS}),\;
2 H_{NN}^{-1} \bigr), \\
R_i &= H_{NN}^{-1} H_{NS} ,
\end{aligned}$$

so the posterior covariance of all random effects of the group, `fit$etaCov`, has the blocks

$$\Sigma_{NN} = 2 H_{NN}^{-1} + R_i \Sigma_{SS} R_i^\top, \qquad \Sigma_{NS} = -R_i \Sigma_{SS} ,$$

with $\Sigma_{SS}$ that of the sparse coordinates above; `se` of `fit$random` is the square root of
its diagonal. $\Omega$ has no M-step here: it moves with the fixed parameters.

By Fisher's identity the same statistics give the gradient in the hyperparameters: at the current
point the derivative of $-2 \log I$ is that of $-2Q$,

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial (-2Q)}{\partial \rho} &= -2 \Bigl( \frac{\bar n}{\rho} - \frac{n - \bar n}{1 - \rho} \Bigr), \\
\frac{\partial (-2Q)}{\partial \tau} &= 2 \Bigl( \frac{\bar n}{\tau} - \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^3} \Bigr),
\end{aligned}$$

$-2$ times the sums over the groups of the derivatives of the factors. The gradient of the
marginal in $\tau$ adds the shift of the mode (section [Exact gradient](#exact-gradient)); $\rho$
does not move the mode. The M-steps set both derivatives of $-2Q$ to zero at fixed statistics.

### M-steps

The closed-form M-step of a hyperparameter $h$ minimises $-2Q(h)$, the expected complete-data
$-2 \log$ prior of the random effects with their structure, at the current posterior moments: the
complete data are $(\eta, z)$ for the spike and slab (section [E-step](#e-step)) and the partition
with the cluster values for the Dirichlet process. With $n$ the number of deviations of a term,
groups times symbols, $\bar n$ the expected number of slab deviations or of clusters off the
population value, and $\mathbb{E} \sum v^2$ the expected sum of their squared values,

$$\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= \frac{n}{\sum \mathbb{E} \lvert \eta \rvert}, &
\tau^2 &= \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\bar n}, \\
\rho &= \frac{\bar n}{n}, &
\bar n &= \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + i} ,
\end{aligned}$$

the last one, for the concentration of the Dirichlet process, summed over the symbols $k$ of the
term; its left side increases in $\alpha$, and Newton's method on $\log \alpha$ solves it.

Near the optimum such a step is a gradient step scaled by the complete-data information
$\mathcal{I}_c$, the information the deviations would give if they were observed, while the data
hold only $\mathcal{I}_{\text{obs}} = \mathcal{I}_c - \mathcal{I}_{\text{mis}}$; per iteration the
error shrinks by the fraction of missing information [@dempster1977maximum], the matrix

$$\mathcal{I}_c^{-1} \mathcal{I}_{\text{mis}} .$$

For a strength estimated from a few groups the rate is close to one. A Newton step on the curvature
of $-2Q$ at the current point is no better far from the optimum: on the unbounded scale
$u = \log \lambda$ the M-step lies at $u^* = \log(n / \sum \mathbb{E} \lvert \eta \rvert)$, the
Newton step is $e^{u^* - u} - 1$, $-1$ where $u^*$ lies five below and $147$ where it lies five
above.

### Joint trust region

`em()` moves all parameters in one trust region: the fixed parameters, and the hyperparameters on
their unbounded scale $u$, $\log \lambda$, $\log \tau$, $\log \alpha$ and
$\operatorname{logit} \rho$, with the exact gradient of the marginal. For the fixed parameters the
model Hessian is the Schur complement over all random effects, the sparse ones at the curvature of
their posterior: a factor with posterior covariance $\Sigma$ and data curvature $\tilde H_{ff}$ of
$-2 \log L$ gets the prior curvature $2 \Sigma^{-1} - \tilde H_{ff}$, so that its block after the normal
coordinates are eliminated is $2 \Sigma^{-1}$; under expectation consistent the prior curvature is
that of the sites, $2 \operatorname{diag}(\Lambda)$. The blocks of the data Hessian are all of one
kind: Gauss-Newton under forward over reverse, whose parameter block is Gauss-Newton, so that the
Schur complement is positive semidefinite; exact with second-order sensitivities. A Schur complement
of a Gauss-Newton parameter block and exact rows in the random effects can be far from definite.
The exact rows enter the gradient and the shift of the mode. With normal random effects alone this
is the Schur complement of FOCEI. The Schur complement over the free
modes alone has no curvature in a fixed parameter whose deviations are free under a Laplace prior,
and jumps to that of the data where the deviations sit at zero.

For every hyperparameter the model Hessian is the secant of the complete-data gradient to its
M-step,

$$\kappa_h = \frac{\partial_u (-2Q)}{u - u^*},$$

with the derivatives of $-2Q$ on the unbounded scale

$$\partial_u (-2Q) = \begin{cases}
2 \bigl( \lambda \sum \mathbb{E} \lvert \eta \rvert - n \bigr) & \text{for } \lambda, \\
2 \bigl( \bar n - \mathbb{E} \sum v^2 / \tau^2 \bigr) & \text{for } \tau, \\
-2 \, (\bar n - n \rho) & \text{for } \rho, \\
-2 \bigl( \bar n - \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha / (\alpha + i) \bigr) & \text{for } \alpha .
\end{cases}$$

$-2Q$ is convex in $u$ for all four, so $\kappa_h > 0$. Where $u = u^*$, $\kappa_h$ is the curvature
of $-2Q$, the complete-data information on the scale of $-2 \log L$,

$$\partial_u^2 (-2Q) = \begin{cases}
2 \lambda \sum \mathbb{E} \lvert \eta \rvert & \text{for } \lambda, \\
4\, \mathbb{E} \sum v^2 / \tau^2 & \text{for } \tau, \\
2 n \rho (1 - \rho) & \text{for } \rho, \\
2 \sum_k \sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha\, i / (\alpha + i)^2 & \text{for } \alpha ,
\end{cases}$$

and $\kappa_h$ is at least $10^{-8}$. The gradient of the marginal in $u$ is that of $-2Q$ at the
current point (section [E-step](#e-step)) plus the term of the shift of the mode, so a Newton step
on $\kappa_h$ alone moves $u$ by

$$\Delta u = -\frac{1}{\kappa_h} \frac{\partial (-2 \log L)}{\partial u}
= u^* - u - \frac{1}{\kappa_h}\, \nabla_{\hat\eta} (-2 \log L)^\top \frac{d \hat\eta}{d u} ,$$

$\nabla_{\hat\eta} (-2 \log L)$ the derivative of the marginal in the mode at fixed parameters and
$d \hat\eta / d u$ the shift of the mode of section [Exact gradient](#exact-gradient). For $\rho$
and $\alpha$ the mode does not move, and the step is the exact M-step. For $\tau$ and $\lambda$ it
adds the second term, which vanishes where the data term is exactly quadratic in the random
effects, the expansion then being independent of the mode.

A BFGS correction from the accepted steps learns the missing information and the curvature between
fixed parameters and hyperparameters [@lange1995quasi; @jamshidian1997acceleration]: every step
between two points that lowered $-2 \log L$ updates the model Hessian by BFGS with the change of
the gradient along it; a pair whose inner product is at most $10^{-8}$ times the product of their
norms is skipped, and an update that would leave the model indefinite drops the correction. Far
from the optimum the correction is small, and a step is an EM step in the hyperparameters and a
Gauss-Newton step in the fixed parameters, at one evaluation of the marginal; near the optimum the model approaches the
Hessian of the marginal and the steps converge superlinearly. The model has the gradient of the
marginal and a bounded Hessian, which suffices for the convergence of a trust region
[@conn2000trust], and the ratio of actual to predicted reduction sets the step: there is no number
of EM iterations to choose.

The trust region stops at a predicted reduction below `mtol`; a run that stops short of it, at its
iteration limit or after rejected steps, starts again with a fresh correction as long as the runs
lower $-2 \log L$ by more than `mtol`. A multistart guards against local optima; `msem()` perturbs
strengths, concentrations and slab standard deviations on the log scale, slab probabilities on the
logit scale. Neither model Hessian is the Hessian of the marginal, which would need the curvature of
the integral over the sparse coordinates: such a fit reports none, `fit$hessian` is `NULL`, and its
standard errors come from the scores of the groups (section [Standard errors](#standard-errors)).

### Settings

| entry of `control$laplace` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `maxOuter` | `200` | the iterations of the joint trust region, over all its runs |
| `trustControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `ftol = 1e-10`, `mtol = 1e-5` | the joint trust region, as in `trust()` |

Other entries are an error. The fit of the compounds sets the tolerances of `trustControl` to those
of [chapter 1](guide-model.html), above the error the solver leaves in the value and the gradient.

## Reported structure

The fit reports the most probable structure: for the spike and slab the most probable subset of
every factor, for the Dirichlet process the most probable partition, from the partition recursion
with the maximum in place of the sum. Deviations in the spike are exactly zero. A slab deviation
is the slab mean given the most probable subset, at the precision and centre at which its factor is
integrated: in a joint factor $\mu_{F^*} = V_{F^*} b_{F^*}$, $F^*$ the most probable subset of the
factor, the posterior mean given the subset, exact without other sparse coordinates; for a
coordinate alone, and for every coordinate under expectation consistent, the slab mean
$\mu = V a\, m$ of section [E-step](#e-step) where $1 - p_0 > \tfrac12$, at the cavity under
expectation consistent, so that it is not conditioned on the structure of the others. Every free cluster has
its posterior mean given the most probable partition, and Laplace deviations are their joint
mode. `fit$random` has a row per group and random effect:

- `mode`, this value;
- `se`, the posterior standard deviation, over spike and slab together;
- for spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process random effects `cluster`, 0 for the population value and
  1, 2, ... for the deviating groups or the clusters of a symbol in the order of the groups, and
  `p0`, the posterior probability of a deviation of zero;
- `data`, where some random effects reach no data of their group, whether each does.

Before the fit, `em()` follows every sparse random effect of a group through the parameter
transformations, the steady states, the right-hand sides and events of the ODE, the observables and
the error model to the names measured in the conditions of the group, a search in the graph of
their symbols. Every expression is read with the names that are 0 in the condition set to 0: a
product with a factor 0 vanishes, and a state that starts at 0, whose right-hand side vanishes with
the other zeros and that no event moves stays 0 for all time, by uniqueness of the solution, and
passes nothing on. A root of a steady state depends on an input only through the states whose
equations or conservation rows the input reaches, directly or through moved states; the others
solve a subsystem without the input, whose solution does not move where it has full structural
rank, and the search falls back to every root where it does not. Where the graph finds no path,
the sensitivity is 0 for every value of the parameters. One that reaches none rests at 0 with its
prior: its mode is not searched, it leaves
the integral, whose factor is 1 there, and it does not enter the updates of its hyperparameters. It
is reported with its prior standard deviation and, for the spike and slab, $p_0 = 1 - \rho$; a
Dirichlet-process group without data leaves the partition, which leaves the others unchanged, as
the Ewens prior of a subset of the groups is that of the subset. Without this the data-free
coordinates would be flat directions of the mode and of the integral.

`fit$strengths` lists the Laplace strengths, `fit$slab` the probabilities, concentrations and slab
standard deviations, each with the symbols of its term, its estimate and whether it was fixed.

The sum over the structures is exact or expectation consistent; the data term in the random effects
of a structure is its Laplace approximation at the joint mode, as in FOCEI.

## Standard errors

With Laplace and spike-and-slab random effects the marginal is a sum over the independent groups
and the conditions without random effects, $-2 \log L = -2 \sum_i \log L_i + D_0$, with $L_i$
the approximate marginal likelihood of group $i$. The mode, the
curvature and the integral of a group depend on its data alone, and the shift of the mode with the
parameters is block diagonal by groups, so the exact gradient of the marginal splits into the exact
gradients $-2 \nabla \log L_i$ of the groups. With the scores $s_i = \nabla \log L_i$ and their
mean $\bar s$, the empirical information is

$$\mathcal{I} = \frac{G}{G - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{G} (s_i - \bar s)(s_i - \bar s)^\top + \tfrac12 H_0 ,$$

$H_0$ the Hessian of $D_0$, which also holds the priors and other terms of the objective.
`fit$information` holds it and `vcov()` inverts it. At the optimum the scores sum to
$\tfrac12 \nabla D_0$, and the centring removes that direction exactly: the first term has rank
at most $G - 1$. The information needs more groups than parameters, or $H_0$ for the directions the
scores leave out; where it does not span every direction, `vcov()` is an error and the standard
errors are `NA`. In the fit of the compounds the five compounds give a first term of rank at most
four, and the conditions without a compound and the prior give the other directions. Under
`dirichletProcess()` the partition couples the groups, the marginal is no sum over groups, and a fit
has neither a Hessian nor an empirical information; `confint(method = "profile")` gives intervals.

## Dirichlet-process random effects

`gr(group, dist = dirichletProcess())` lets the groups of a symbol share deviations: the groups and
the population value, the anchor, form clusters; the cluster of the anchor has deviation zero, and
every other cluster one common deviation from the slab $\mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. The fit estimates
the concentration $\alpha$ and $\tau$ by marginal maximum likelihood, in one fit without a penalty
to scan. The structure a fit reports is that of the spike and slab with clusters in place of single
deviations; the compounds of this chapter are fitted without it.

### Ewens prior

The partitions $\mathcal{C}$ of the $G$ groups and the anchor have the Ewens distribution
[@ewens1972sampling] of the Chinese restaurant process with concentration $\alpha$ and the anchor
seated first: a group joins an existing cluster with probability proportional to its size, the
anchor counted, or opens a new one with probability proportional to $\alpha$,

$$\Pr(\mathcal{C}) = \frac{\alpha^{\lvert \mathcal{C} \rvert - 1} \prod_{T \in \mathcal{C}} (\lvert T \rvert - 1)!}
{\prod_{i=1}^{G} (\alpha + i)} ,$$

$\lvert \mathcal{C} \rvert$ the number of clusters and $\lvert T \rvert$ their sizes. The prior depends on the
sizes only: it is exchangeable in the groups, independent of their order and of the data, and
consistent in $G$, so that leaving out a group gives the prior of the others. $\alpha \to 0$ puts
every group at the population value, $\alpha \to \infty$ every group in a cluster of its own; the
expected number of free clusters, those off the population value, is
$\sum_{i=1}^{G} \alpha / (\alpha + i)$.

### Partition sum

The data term is expanded as for the other sparse random effects, around the mode under the slab
alone. Per symbol, on the factors $(a_i, m_i)$ of its $G$ groups, precision and centre, a cluster
$T$ with the sums

$$A_T = \sum_{i \in T} a_i, \qquad B_T = \sum_{i \in T} a_i m_i, \qquad C_T = \sum_{i \in T} a_i m_i^2$$

has the weight

$$w(T) = (\lvert T \rvert - 1)!\; e^{-C_T / 2}$$

if it holds the anchor, and otherwise, integrating its common value over the slab,

$$w(T) = \alpha\, (\lvert T \rvert - 1)!\; \bigl(1 + \tau^2 A_T\bigr)^{-1/2}
\exp\Bigl( -\frac{C_T}{2} + \frac{B_T^2}{2 (A_T + \tau^{-2})} \Bigr) .$$

The sum over all set partitions is a recursion over the subsets of the $G + 1$ elements: with
$\mathcal{Z}(X)$ the sum over the partitions of a subset $X$ of the products of their cluster
weights,

$$\mathcal{Z}(X) = \sum_{T \subseteq X,\ \min X \in T} w(T)\, \mathcal{Z}(X \setminus T), \qquad
I = \frac{\mathcal{Z}(U)}{\prod_{i=1}^{G} (\alpha + i)} ,$$

$U$ the full set, $3^{G+1}$ terms, exact for up to 14 groups. The posterior probability that $T$ is
a cluster is $w(T)\, \mathcal{Z}(U \setminus T) / \mathcal{Z}(U)$; given that, the value of a free cluster is normal
with mean $B_T / (A_T + \tau^{-2})$ and variance $1 / (A_T + \tau^{-2})$. The posterior moments of
every group, its $p_0$, the M-step statistics and the derivatives follow from these probabilities.
The most probable partition is the same recursion with the maximum in place of the sum.

### Gradient and M-steps

Fisher's identity gives the derivatives of $\log I$ in $m$, in $a$ and in the hyperparameters from
the posterior moments,

$$\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial \alpha} = \frac{\bar n}{\alpha} - \sum_{i=1}^{G} \frac{1}{\alpha + i},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \log I}{\partial \tau} = -\frac{\bar n}{\tau} + \frac{\mathbb{E} \sum v^2}{\tau^3} ,$$

with $\bar n$ the expected number of free clusters and $\mathbb{E} \sum v^2$ the expected sum of their
squared values; the chain through $\nabla D_i$, $H_i$ and the mode is that of the other sparse
random effects. The mode shifts with $\tau$ through the slab term, not with $\alpha$. The M-steps of
$\tau$ and $\alpha$ are those of the section [M-steps](#m-steps), summed over the symbols of a term,
and they set the curvature of $\alpha$ and $\tau$ in the joint trust region.

### SAEM

The exact partition sum is limited to 14 groups. `method = "saem"` draws the partition instead,
with normal random effects beside the Dirichlet-process ones and no other sparse ones. Every group
starts in a cluster of its own at its mode under the slab alone, so that the sampler merges clusters
rather than finds deviations by draws from the slab. An iteration has these steps:

- **Normal random effects.** Random-walk Metropolis steps, `nMcmc` per iteration, the step size
  adapted during burn-in towards an acceptance of 0.4.
- **Clusters.** One Gibbs sweep per symbol, Neal's algorithm 8 with two auxiliary clusters
  [@neal2000markov]: every group, in random order, leaves its cluster and joins an existing one
  with probability proportional to its size, the anchor counted, times the likelihood of the group
  at the cluster value, or one of two auxiliary clusters with values drawn from the slab, with
  probability proportional to $\alpha / 2$ times the likelihood there. A group alone in its cluster
  offers that value as one of the auxiliary ones. The likelihoods of all groups at one value come
  from one prediction.
- **Cluster values.** Three random-walk Metropolis steps on the values of all clusters at once,
  each accepted on the data of its groups and the slab.
- **A-step and M-steps.** Robbins-Monro averages of the number of free clusters and of the sum of
  their squared values give $\tau$ and $\alpha$ by the M-steps above; during burn-in they change by
  a factor between 0.95 and 1.25 per iteration, and the variances of $\Omega$ shrink by at most
  5 %. $\Omega$, the mu-referenced fixed effects and the other structural parameters move as in the
  SAEM of [chapter 7](guide-nlme.html).

Burn-in ends when no parameter drifts over the last `window` iterations, or after `nBurnin`; the
averaging, with step sizes falling as the iteration number to the power $-0.7$, runs `nEM` iterations, and the estimate is the
mean of the iterates after its first `window`. `converged` says whether the burn-in ended by the
drift test. The reported structure is the most frequent partition of the draws after that window,
its cluster values averaged over the draws with that partition, and $p_0$ of a group the share of
those draws in which it sits at the population value.

### Importance sampling

The $-2 \log L$ of an SAEM fit comes from sequential importance sampling under the expansion
[@liu1996nonparametric]. A particle seats the groups one after the other; group $i$ joins a cluster
of every symbol, an existing one or a new one, with probability proportional to the Ewens prior
times its predictive given the groups seated before, the cluster values of the particle having a
joint normal posterior. With $\mathcal{C}_{i-1}$ the partition after $i - 1$ groups and
$Z(\mathcal{C})$ the integral of the seated factors under it, the weight of a particle is the
product of the normalisers,

$$\zeta = \prod_{i=1}^{G} \sum_{T} \Pr(T \mid \mathcal{C}_{i-1})\,
\frac{Z(\mathcal{C}_{i-1} + T)}{Z(\mathcal{C}_{i-1})} ,$$

the sum over the seats $T$ of group $i$, a cluster of every symbol, existing or new. Its mean
$\bar\zeta$ over $M$ particles is unbiased for $I$, and the spread gives the standard error of
$-2 \log L$,

$$\texttt{valueSE} = \frac{2\, \operatorname{sd}(\zeta)}{\sqrt{M}\, \bar\zeta} ,$$

by the delta method on $\log \bar\zeta$. The symbols of a group are seated together on its full
precision $P_i$, so no factorisation enters. `control$saem$particles` sets $M$, default 500. An
SAEM fit has no gradient, Hessian or empirical information.

## Summary

- A spike-and-slab random effect over a grouping gives, per group and parameter, the posterior
  probability $p_0$ of no change, with the probability and the spread of the changes estimated from
  all groups together.
- `em()` integrates Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process random effects on the quadratic
  expansion of the data at the joint mode: normal coordinates by the Schur complement, every factor
  exactly, spike-and-slab random effects of a group jointly by a pruned sum over their subsets,
  coupled factors by expectation consistent.
- Fixed effects and hyperparameters move in one trust region with the exact gradient, the
  hyperparameters on the secant to their M-steps; standard errors come from the scores of the
  groups.
- Dirichlet-process random effects sum exactly over the partitions of up to 14 groups;
  `method = "saem"` draws the partitions of more and reports $-2 \log L$ with its standard error.
